reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: The commonest malignant ovarian germ-cell tumour, arising predominantly in adolescents and young women
Regarded as the ovarian counterpart of testicular seminoma, sharing similar histology and marked radiosensitivity and chemosensitivity
Often presents as a rapidly enlarging solid pelvic mass, sometimes with acute pain from torsion or rupture
Serum lactate dehydrogenase is frequently raised, and modest beta-hCG elevation can occur when syncytiotrophoblast-like giant cells are present, whereas AFP is characteristically normal
Associated with an isochromosome 12p abnormality, mirroring the cytogenetics of testicular germ-cell tumours
Has a particular association with dysgenetic gonads (for example in gonadal dysgenesis with a Y chromosome), where a gonadoblastoma may progress to dysgerminoma
Because it is highly responsive to platinum-based chemotherapy, fertility-sparing surgery with preservation of the uterus and contralateral ovary is often feasible even in advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Dysgerminoma is a malignant germ-cell tumour composed of primitive germ cells that have not differentiated towards embryonic or extra-embryonic tissues, so its cells resemble the primordial oocytes and mirror testicular seminoma. Sheets and nests of uniform cells with clear cytoplasm are separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes, and scattered syncytiotrophoblast-like cells may secrete small amounts of beta-hCG. The tumour commonly shows gain of the short arm of chromosome 12 as an isochromosome 12p. In individuals with dysgenetic gonads carrying Y-chromosome material, a precursor gonadoblastoma can give rise to dysgerminoma, which is why karyotyping and consideration of gonadectomy are important in such patients. The tumour is intrinsically radiosensitive and chemosensitive, a key determinant of its favourable outlook.
additionalDifferentials: Other malignant germ-cell tumours (yolk sac tumour, immature teratoma, embryonal carcinoma)
Small cell carcinoma of the ovary
additionalInvestigations: Serum LDH, beta-hCG, and AFP to characterise the germ-cell tumour and monitor response
Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound of a solid ovarian mass
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for staging including nodal assessment
Karyotype or genetic testing, particularly in young patients or where gonadal dysgenesis is suspected
Histology with immunohistochemistry (e.g. OCT4, SALL4, c-KIT/CD117)
Assessment of the contralateral ovary given the possibility of bilateral disease
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging solid ovarian mass in an adolescent or young woman
Acute pain from torsion or rupture of a germ-cell tumour
A dysgenetic gonad containing Y-chromosome material at risk of malignant change
Rising tumour markers indicating progression or a mixed germ-cell component
reference.prognosis: Excellent, particularly for early-stage disease, and even advanced or recurrent tumours frequently achieve cure because of high sensitivity to platinum-based chemotherapy; fertility can often be preserved.
pitfalls: Assuming a solid ovarian mass in a young woman is benign and delaying diagnosis
Failing to karyotype patients with features of gonadal dysgenesis, missing a Y-chromosome cancer risk
Interpreting a raised AFP as consistent with pure dysgerminoma rather than a mixed germ-cell tumour
Performing unnecessarily radical surgery when fertility-sparing treatment would suffice
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Perform fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with surgical staging as the mainstay for disease apparently confined to one ovary
Give platinum-based combination chemotherapy such as bleomycin, etoposide and cisplatin for advanced, metastatic or recurrent disease, exploiting marked chemosensitivity
Preserve the uterus and contralateral ovary wherever feasible, given the young age at presentation, and discuss fertility preservation before treatment
Karyotype young patients and, where dysgenetic gonads carry Y-chromosome material, perform bilateral gonadectomy because of gonadoblastoma and malignancy risk
Monitor treatment response and detect relapse with serial tumour markers (lactate dehydrogenase and beta-hCG) and imaging surveillance
Manage within a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team, assessing the contralateral ovary for bilateral disease
Reserve radiotherapy for selected chemoresistant situations given the tumour's radiosensitivity
